Using a mystical deck and a healthy dose of logic, you can predict each others' fates and escape unscathed. The Shipwreck Arcana is a compact, co-operative game of deduction, evaluation, and logic. Each player's doom constantly changes as they draw numbered fate tiles from the bag. By choosing which fate to give up and which card to play it on, you can give your allies enough information to identify the fate you're holding...which is important, as the active player cannot communicate with their allies during their turn! This is a cooperative game; the players win or lose together. If the players reach 7 doom (as indicated by the red tracking token around The Hours ), they lose. (In the The Restless Hours variant, the players lose if the deck is empty and they need to draw a card.) If the players score 7 points (as indicated by the green tracking token), they win. Rules summary The official rules from Meromorph Games are available on their website . Each fate is a token numbered 1 through 7. There are three of each fate (so, 21 fate tokens total) in a bag that players drawn from. Discarded fates are returned to the bag. Each player has a number-line of tokens numbered 1 through 7 in their color. A player cannot interact with their own number-line; it's used by the rest of the group to help keep track of what the group knows. Number-lines have no direct effect on gameplay. Four arcana cards are active (in play) at any given time. Fates played on the arcana cards are called visible fates . Whenever an arcana card is removed from play, any visible fates on it are discarded and returned to the bag, and it is replaced with the top card of the deck. The top card of the deck is always face up, but that card is not active, and fates may not be played on it. Each fate token has a number of hours ("pips", or ♢) shown on its right side. (Fates numbered 1 through 3 have one pip; 4 through 6 have two pips; and 7 has three pips.). Each arcana card has a duration , indicated by the number of moons shown near its bottom edge. When the number of hours (pips) of visible fates on an arcana card is greater than or equal to its duration, that arcana card will fade at the end of the turn. Faded arcana cards become single-use faded powers that can help the group. See "Faded powers" for more information. To the left of the active arcana cards is The Hours card. Players play a fate on The Hours if they cannot play a fate anywhere else. At the end of a turn, fates on The Hours move to the leftmost arcana card (which may cause that card to fade). Tracking tokens around The Hours are used to indicate the group's current doom (red token) and score (green token). Turn On each turn, one player (or, in the Two-player Challenge Variant , one hand) is the active player. The rest of the players are "the group". The active player may not communicate with the group in any way except by using faded powers and playing a fate. Each turn is split into several phases. The active player draws new fates until they have two in their hand. These are secret from the other players. The active player plays one fate on an arcana card, obeying its text. If the player cannot play a fate on any arcana card, they must play on on The Hours. The group is allowed to discuss openly and then may predict (guess) what the active player's remaining fate is (or may pass). They may use the active player's number-line to keep track of which fate numbers they think the active player could have. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Dry co-op game. Theme is non-existent that it's pretty much an abstract game. No tension. No exciting moments. Dull.  Art is nice though

[Rating: 1/10] Very logical kinds of puzzles, that usually come down to 50/50 guessing in the end. Reminds me of Hanabi but with less cleverness and more noisiness.

[Rating: 2/10] Kind of easy, super-quarterbacky, and saddled with the most ridiculous premise, but still kinda neat.

[Rating: 2/10] An embarrassing design that isn't a game, it's just a shared logic puzzle. If everyone interprets the cards properly, then it's just luck whether the tile you pull can be determined by the visible objectives.

[Rating: 3/10] The logic is too easy in that either the other player plays correctly and you reach a simple conclusion, or the other player plays suboptimally/there is no optimal play, and you don't do as well.

[Rating: 3/10] This is another in the line of "no-talking" cooperatives.  The game has its clever moments, but it is generally much too easy, even without the additional powers gained from fulfilling cards.

[Rating: 3/10] This game felt almost trivial. We played this a couple of times with differing player counts, but each time a clue was given, that clue could be posed in a unique way so that the person would immediately know, what their number is. A cooperative game that is no challenge? No thanks.

[Rating: 3/10] This was an arithmetic game more than anything else, and not a really fascinating one.

[Rating: 3/10] Most games I played of this just had one correct choice and you just waited for the player to find it.  Or you had no correct option and lost.

[Rating: 3/10] Not much of a game, and it seems like your chances of winning are mostly determined by the mix of cards that you get. Some card combinations can be impossible, while others make the game trivial.

[Rating: 3/10] Try to solve a chain of little logic puzzles in a randomly highly favourable or absurdly unfavourable environment. Did like the illustration style that is somewhat reminiscent of Mignola.
